transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-11-28 20:00 UTC | Duration: 45m
Attendees: Sienna Park (Redwood), Marcus Nguyen (Redwood SE), Ari Patel (Redwood Marketing); Dr. Maya Patel (Lumina Health), Carlos Rios (Lumina Product Marketing), Jen Park (Lumina Eng Manager)
Recording note: podcast-style customer interview, informal, permission requested for publishing.

Summary: Quick conversational interview about Lumina Health's experience moving inference to Redwood; focus on performance, cost, and product impact. Several anecdotes about integration and go-live. Action items captured at end.

00:00 - Sienna: Hey everyone, thanks so much for joining, really appreciate you carving out time for this - I'm Sienna from Redwood and I'm gonna kick us off with a couple of warm up q's, then Ari will do the marketing-y stuff, and Maya, Carlos, Jen thanks for being here.
00:18 - Maya: Yeah thanks, excited.
00:22 - Sienna: Cool. First question for you Maya, can you just tell us in your own words what problem you were trying to solve before Redwood?
00:30 - Maya: Sure, so at Lumina we were trying to get generative summaries and triage into clinicians' workflows. We had a few prototypes on-prem but they were slow and expensive to scale, so clinical ops wouldn't adopt it because, you know, latency and reliability matter when a nurse is triaging.
00:52 - Carlos: And also the audit and compliance angle was huge for us, lots of golden record needs and we couldn't ship until that was solved.
01:05 - Sienna: Yeah totally. When did you first try Redwood and what made you pick it over others?
01:12 - Maya: We did a bunch of benchmarks in mid-2024, we tested a mix of managed APIs and our own infra. Redwood's performance numbers, especially on tail latency and continuous batching, were compelling. Plus the dedicated/reserved capacity offering - sorry the, the Redwood dedicate — small transcription glitch there — but basically the dedicated option let us hit our SLOs.
01:37 - Marcus (SE): Maya if you don't mind me asking, what were the SLO targets you needed?
01:42 - Maya: We were targeting 95th percentile under 300ms for the 512-token summaries in our staging workload; in production we accepted some variance but we wanted 95th under 500ms.
01:55 - Marcus: Ok that's helpful, thanks. We actually ran a short bench with Lumina's sample prompts and saw consistent 95p around 220-260ms on dedicated pools.
02:06 - Jen: That matched our internal testing once we switched to Redwood's runtime. Also the KV cache helped a lot with repeated prefixes for patient notes.
02:18 - Ari (Marketing): Can I jump in with a story — we loved the anecdote where the nursing manager said the summaries saved them an extra 10 minutes per chart, is that right?
02:27 - Maya: Yeah that's true, it's anecdotal but she said throughput improved and the staff felt less burnout for repeat tasks. We then validated in a small pilot — the median time per patient note review dropped by about 8 minutes.
02:40 - Carlos: We correlated that with a 12% increase in throughput for the triage team across a 2-week pilot.
02:48 - Sienna: Those are great numbers. Were there concerns around data residency, SOC 2, or encryption during selection?
02:55 - Maya: Absolutely. We needed SOC 2 and audit logs, SSO (SAML), and encrypted-at-rest with customer-managed keys. Redwood's Private/VPC story and KMS integrations were crucial — we had to get security signoff.
03:12 - Marcus: And on the engineering side we worked with Lumina to map the network flows for VPC peering; there were a couple of config gotchas but nothing major.
03:22 - Jen: Right, initial setup had one routing rule that blocked outbound metrics but once Marcus pointed it out we were good.
03:30 - Sienna: Nice. Ari, any marketing-specific questions for quotes or permissions?
03:35 - Ari: Yeah, two quick things. One, do you have a short soundbite about impact for the opening of the case study? Two, are you comfortable with us publishing a joint case study and a short podcast episode?
03:46 - Maya: For a bite — "Redwood made inference predictable for clinical workflows, cutting median review time and reducing friction for adoption." And yes we are comfortable pending legal signoff.
03:58 - Carlos: Legal will need to review, but we've done these before so shouldn't be a big blocker.
04:05 - Ari: Great — we'll send the permission form and a draft transcript after today's call.
04:10 - Sienna: Sounds good. A couple of tech clarifications we might include in the write-up: you used the dedicated pool for the pilot and then shifted some non-critical workloads to hosted to save cost, is that fair?
04:21 - Jen: Yeah, exactly. We pinned the critical triage to dedicated to guarantee latency and routed lower-priority bulk processing to hosted endpoints during off-peak hours. It was a good tradeoff.
04:33 - Marcus: We also recommended specific quantization and batching settings — a mixed-precision q4 model for inference and per-route batching cap around 32 for that workload.
04:42 - Maya: That detail helped the cost numbers, which I'd like to share — we saw roughly 40% unit cost reduction versus our prior self-hosted setup when accounting for operations and GPU utilization.
04:55 - Carlos: And importantly the cost per patient triage went down which made the ROI argument easy for product leadership.
05:03 - Sienna: Awesome. Anything surprising about the rollout or adoption?
05:08 - Maya: The surprise was speed of clinical adoption; once latency was solved they actually used it more than we expected. A small UX change (the one-click summary) made a big difference.
05:18 - Ari: Love that — UX + infra = adoption.
05:21 - Sienna: Okay quick segue: the legal and compliance checklist — do you want us to send the SOC 2 and penetration test reports to your security contact?
05:29 - Carlos: Yes please, send to security@luminahealth.com and I'll loop legal.
05:34 - Sienna: Will do.
05:36 - Marcus: One quick note on benchmarks: we'll attach the bench spreadsheet and the sample prompts we used — feel free to publish as an appendix if you'd like.
05:44 - Maya: That would be useful for our internal documentation too.
05:48 - Ari: On the publication side, what timeframe works for you? We were thinking publish mid-December.
05:53 - Carlos: Mid-December works if we can close metrics by Dec 5.
05:58 - Sienna: Great. Final segment: any gotchas to call out for other customers listening?
06:04 - Jen: Make sure you validate tokenization differences for clinical abbreviations; in our first run punctuation and token splits produced slightly different summaries until we normalized prompts.
06:15 - Marcus: Also watch out for long-tail sequence lengths, you might want to set a hard limit or special route for extremely long notes.
06:22 - Maya: And don't underestimate the importance of SSO and audit logs for clinical ops — they won't adopt without those.
06:30 - Ari: Perfect. We'll do a brief recap and next steps: Redwood sends draft transcript, permission form, SOC2/pen test links, bench spreadsheet. Lumina provides final metrics and headshot/bio for Maya and Carlos.
06:45 - Carlos: Yep.
06:47 - Sienna: Thanks again everyone, we'll follow up via email and drop the docs in the shared drive. Any last comments?
06:55 - Maya: Thanks, excited to see the draft.
07:00 - Sienna: Okay we're off — end recording.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings (Redwood dedicate => dedicated), filler words present, occasional speaker label ambiguity; timestamps are approximate.

References / artifacts mentioned: deck: https://redwood.app/share/lumina-deck (placeholder), bench spreadsheet (attached in follow-up), permission form (to be sent).

End of transcript.
